question: Which statement best describes Interruptible rendering?
options: In React 18, multiple state updates are batched into a single re-render automatically — not just inside event handlers, but also in promises, timeouts, and native event callbacks. Before 18, updates outside React event handlers triggered separate renders. Batching reduces wasted renders; you can opt out for a specific update with flushSync when you truly need a synchronous DOM update.

Internally React tags every update with a priority 'lane' and uses a cooperative scheduler to decide what to work on next. The scheduler periodically checks a time budget and yields to the browser so it can paint and process input. Higher-priority lanes (urgent) jump ahead of lower-priority lanes (transitions), which is the mechanism that keeps interactions responsive.

React classifies updates into urgent (typing, clicking, hovering) and non-urgent transitions (filtering a list, navigating). Urgent updates must feel instant, so they preempt transitions. You opt a state update into a transition with startTransition or useTransition, and React schedules it at lower priority so it can be interrupted by anything urgent.

The core capability that makes concurrency possible: React breaks reconciliation into small units of work and can pause partway through, hand control back to the browser, then resume or abandon the work. This is what keeps a slow render from monopolizing the main thread. The catch is that a render function may execute more than once before (or without ever) committing, so it must be pure.

Tearing is a consistency hazard unique to concurrent rendering: because a render can pause, an external mutable store could change mid-render, leaving some components showing the old value and others the new one. useSyncExternalStore is the official hook that lets external stores subscribe and read a consistent snapshot so React never commits torn UI. React's own useState is immune; only external mutable sources are at risk.

Time slicing is the practical effect of interruptible rendering: React spreads a large render across multiple frames instead of doing it in one long blocking task. Between slices it yields so the browser can handle clicks, keystrokes, and paints. This does not reduce total work — the same rendering happens — it just stops any single chunk from freezing the page.

A hook that lets a value lag behind its source at low priority, useful when you don't own the setter or want to derive expensive output from a trailing value. React renders the urgent value immediately and produces the deferred version when there's spare time, interrupting that work if a newer value arrives. Comparing the deferred value to the live one tells you whether the UI is stale.

question: Which statement best describes Tearing and useSyncExternalStore?
options: Because concurrent rendering may run a component multiple times and discard partial trees, render functions must be pure: same inputs produce the same output with no observable side effects. Mutating external state, logging, or writing to the DOM during render can run twice or for a tree that never commits. StrictMode double-invokes renders in development specifically to surface these impurities; side effects belong in useEffect, which runs after commit.
